hook_text: In 1956, twenty thousand women stood outside the seat of government in total silence, and it was louder than any speech.
clip_script: 9 August 1956. Pretoria. The Union Buildings. Twenty thousand women have come from every corner of the country. By train. By bus. On foot. Some with babies on their backs. They are here because the government wants black women to carry passes. A pass could tear a mother from her children. Four leaders, African, white, Indian and coloured, carry the petitions to the Prime Minister's office. He isn't there. They leave the petitions anyway. Then Lilian Ngoyi raises her hand. Twenty thousand women fall silent. For thirty minutes, not a sound. Fists raised. Then a song rises: you strike a woman, you strike a rock. The passes still came. But the women had been heard. Today, 9 August is National Women's Day.
visual_style: Black-and-white photographs of the crowd filling the Union Buildings amphitheatre; women in traditional dress and Congress colours; the four leaders carrying bundles of petitions; raised fists in silence; portraits of Lilian Ngoyi and Helen Joseph; a modern Women's Day celebration.
pacing: Building steadily, then a long pause for the silence, then the song.
